items.title: How to read an unseen passage (the two-read method)
items.body:
The English qualifying paper gives a **~250-word passage followed by short-answer questions (15 marks)**. Do not read word-by-word; read with a plan.

**Read 1 — for the gist (skim).** Read quickly to get the topic and the author's overall point. Do not stop at hard words.

**Read the questions.** Now you know what to hunt for. Underline the key word in each question (a name, a date, a term).

**Read 2 — for detail (scan).** Go back to the exact lines that answer each question. For a detail question, the answer is *stated*; locate it. For inference/tone, read the lines *around* the clue.

**Answer in your own words, briefly.** Short-answer means one or two sentences — no copying whole lines, no padding.

| Question type | Where the answer lives |
|---|---|
| Main idea / title | Whole passage; often first/last line |
| Explicit detail | One specific line — scan for the keyword |
| Inference | Implied by lines, not stated |
| Vocabulary-in-context | The sentence around the word |
| Tone / purpose | The author's word choice |
keyPoints: The RC item is a ~250-word passage + short-answer questions worth 15 marks (SSC standard).
Use two reads: Read 1 skim for the gist, Read 2 scan for the exact answer lines.
Read the questions before the second read so you know what to look for.
Detail answers are stated in one line; inference/tone answers come from the lines around a clue.
Answer briefly in your own words — do not copy whole sentences.
items.source: APPSC 07/2026 English syllabus — Reading Comprehension; SSC-standard RC method.

items.title: The main RC question types and how to attack each
items.body:
Almost every RC question falls into one of a few types. Recognising the type tells you where to look.

- **Main idea / central theme** — the one point the whole passage develops. Ask: 'What is the author trying to say overall?'
- **Title** — the shortest accurate label for the main idea; not too wide, not too narrow.
- **Explicit detail** — a fact stated in the passage. Scan for the keyword and read that line.
- **Inference** — a conclusion the passage supports but does not state. Stay close to the text; do not import outside knowledge.
- **Vocabulary-in-context** — the meaning a word takes *here*. Substitute each option into the sentence.
- **Tone / attitude** — the author's feeling, shown by word choice (critical, sceptical, appreciative, neutral, ironic). Loaded words such as *so-called*, *much fanfare* or *once again* signal a sceptical, critical tone.
- **Purpose** — *why* a sentence/paragraph is there (to define, contrast, illustrate, introduce). A signpost sentence such as 'consider three factors' looks forward: it introduces and organises what follows; a summary looks back.
- **Pronoun reference** — which noun a word like *it / they / this* points back to. Test each noun: which one can sensibly do or receive the action? ('The committee submitted its report, but she rejected it' → *it* = the report; *she* = the minister.)
- **Fact vs opinion** — a fact can be verified; an opinion is a judgement ('best', 'should').

**Sequence and connectors.** Some questions ask which linking word keeps the ideas in logical order. Match the connector to the relationship:

| Relationship | Connectors |
|---|---|
| Sequence (steps in order) | first, next, then, after that, finally |
| Contrast | however, in contrast, but, on the other hand |
| Concession | nevertheless, even so, although |
| Cause / result | because, so, therefore, as a result |

**Don't confuse:** a list of steps ('First … ___ … Finally') needs a sequence word such as *Next* — not a contrast word such as *However*.
keyPoints: Main idea = the single point the whole passage develops; a supporting detail is narrower.
Inference stays anchored to the text — never add outside knowledge.
Vocabulary-in-context: substitute each option into the sentence and keep the sense.
Tone is revealed by loaded/ironic word choice (e.g. 'so-called').
A fact is verifiable; an opinion uses judgement words like 'best' or 'should'.
Connectors: sequence = first/next/then/finally; contrast = however/in contrast; concession = nevertheless.

items.title: Detail vs inference — the commonest trap
items.body:
Candidates lose marks by confusing what is **stated** with what is merely **suggested**.

**Detail (stated):** the answer is written in the passage; you can point to the exact words. Choose the option that matches the text, not the one that only 'sounds right'.

**Inference (implied):** the passage gives clues; the answer is the safest conclusion those clues support. A good inference needs *no* facts beyond the passage.

**Test for a safe inference:** 'Does the passage give me enough to be sure of this?' If you must assume extra facts, it is a wrong option.

**Distractor traps to avoid:**
- *Too extreme* — words like 'always', 'never', 'only' when the passage is moderate.
- *Out of scope* — true in the real world but never mentioned in the passage.
- *Reversed* — states the opposite of the passage.
- *Half-right* — one clause matches, the other adds a false detail.

**'The author would most likely agree that …'** is an inference about the author's view. Pick the option that follows from the author's argument (for example, if the author says early-schooling money saves money later, the author would call it a wise investment). Reject options that reverse the argument or push it to an extreme ('stop welfare immediately').
keyPoints: Detail answers are stated verbatim; point to the exact line.
A safe inference needs no facts beyond the passage itself.
Reject options that are too extreme (always/never/only) for a moderate passage.
Out-of-scope options can be true in reality yet never appear in the passage — reject them.
Watch half-right options: one clause matches, the other adds a false detail.
'Author would agree' questions: choose the option that follows from the author's argument; reject reversed or extreme options.

items.title: Working out meaning from context
items.body:
You will meet unfamiliar words. You rarely need a dictionary — the sentence usually contains a clue.

**Four context clues:**
1. **Definition/restatement** — the meaning is given nearby, often after a comma or 'that is'. *'She was garrulous, that is, extremely talkative.'*
2. **Contrast** — a signal like *but, however, unlike* points to an opposite. *'He was usually calm, but that day he was livid.'* → livid ≈ very angry.
3. **Example** — items listed after the word reveal it. *'Ungulates such as deer, cattle and horses...'* → ungulates = hoofed animals.
4. **Tone/logic** — the overall sense of the sentence narrows the meaning.

**Method:** replace the word with each option in turn; keep the one that keeps the sentence true and smooth. Beware a word's *common* meaning when the context forces a *different* sense (e.g. 'novel idea' = new, not a book).
keyPoints: Use four context clues: definition, contrast, example, and overall logic/tone.
Contrast signals (but, however, unlike) point to an opposite meaning.
Substitute each option into the sentence and keep the smoothest, truest sense.
The contextual meaning may differ from a word's most common meaning ('novel' = new).

items.title: Writing good short answers (scoring the 15 marks)
items.body:
The paper asks for **short answers**, not option-ticking, so *how* you write matters.

**Do:**
- Answer only what is asked; one or two clear sentences.
- Use your **own words** — paraphrase the passage; a full copied line can lose marks.
- Write a **complete sentence** that would make sense without the question ('The author values green spaces because they cool the air and reduce stress.').
- For a 'why' question, give the reason; for a 'what' question, give the thing.

**Don't:**
- Don't copy a whole paragraph hoping the answer is inside it.
- Don't add your own opinion unless the question asks for it.
- Don't leave a one-word answer where a sentence is expected.

**Marking:** examiners look for the correct point + clear, grammatical English. Accuracy first, then expression.

**Paraphrase (restating in your own words).** A paraphrase keeps the **same meaning and the same scope** but changes the words and structure. Check three things: (1) nothing new is added, (2) nothing important is dropped, (3) the strength of the claim is unchanged ('few X as … as Y' becomes 'Y … more than almost any other X', not 'Y is the only X').

**Don't confuse:** a paraphrase is not a summary (a summary shortens) and not a copy (a copy keeps the words).
keyPoints: Give one or two complete, self-contained sentences per short answer.
Paraphrase in your own words; copying a whole line can lose marks.
Answer exactly what is asked — 'why' wants a reason, 'what' wants the thing.
Do not add personal opinion unless the question requests it.
Marks reward the correct point plus clear, grammatical expression.
Paraphrase = same meaning and scope, different words; add nothing, drop nothing, keep the claim's strength.

items.title: The English paper and the two reading speeds — skimming and scanning
items.body:
**In one line:** the English qualifying paper (150 marks, 180 minutes, SSC standard) gives **one ~250-word passage with short-answer questions for 15 marks** (item 08); you read it twice — once **skimming**, once **scanning**.

**Why it is asked:** comprehension is the most reliable 15 marks in a qualifying paper, and the method decides speed and accuracy.

**The paper at a glance:**
- **10 items, 150 marks, 180 minutes**, medium **English**, **SSC standard**.
- **Qualifying** — marks are **not counted for merit**, but you must score **40% (OC/EWS/Sports), 35% (BC) or 30% (SC/ST/PBD)**.
- Item 08 = **Reading comprehension, ~250 words, short-answer questions, 15 marks**.

**Two reading speeds:**

| Skill | What you do | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| **Skimming** | read fast for the general idea, ignoring details | gist, main idea, title |
| **Scanning** | run the eye down the text for one keyword, name, date or number | detail questions |

**How to do it:**
1. **Skim** the whole passage (about a minute) — topic and the writer's stand.
2. **Read the questions** and underline each keyword.
3. **Scan** back to the line holding each keyword; read the sentences around it.
4. **Write** each answer in one or two complete sentences in your own words.

**Remember it:** *Skim = gist; Scan = spot.*

**Don't confuse:** **skimming** (whole passage, fast, for the idea) with **scanning** (searching for one specific item).
keyPoints: English qualifying paper: 10 items, 150 marks, 180 minutes, SSC standard, medium English.
Item 08 = ~250-word passage + short-answer questions, 15 marks.
Qualifying: not counted for merit; minimum 40% OC/EWS/Sports, 35% BC, 30% SC/ST/PBD.
Skimming = reading fast for the general idea (gist, main idea, title).
Scanning = searching the text for one keyword, name, date or number (detail questions).

items.title: Tone words, author's purpose and passage types
items.body:
**In one line:** tone is the writer's **attitude**, purpose is the writer's **reason for writing**, and the passage type is the **form** the writing takes — each has a small, fixed vocabulary that RC options use.

**Why it is asked:** tone and purpose questions offer four similar-sounding adjectives; knowing their exact meaning removes guesswork.

**Tone words:**

| Tone | Meaning | Signal |
|---|---|---|
| optimistic | hopeful about the future | "will improve", "promising" |
| pessimistic | expecting the worst | "doomed", "bound to fail" |
| sarcastic / ironic | saying the opposite of what is meant, to mock | "so-called", "what a great idea" |
| nostalgic | longing for the past | "those golden days" |
| didactic | teaching a moral lesson | "we must learn", "one should" |
| satirical | mocking folly to correct it | exaggeration of faults |
| objective / neutral | facts without feeling | numbers, plain statements |
| laudatory / appreciative | praising | "remarkable", "admirable" |
| sceptical | doubtful, unconvinced | "yet another", "once again" |

**Author's purpose — the four verbs:** to **inform**, to **persuade**, to **entertain**, to **describe / explain**.

**Passage types:**

| Type | Does what | Clue |
|---|---|---|
| Narrative | tells a story in time order | then, later, one day |
| Descriptive | paints a person, place or scene | sense details |
| Expository | explains a topic with facts | definitions, causes |
| Argumentative | argues a position | should, therefore, however |

**Signal words for relationships:** cause/effect — *because, therefore, as a result*; contrast — *however, whereas, but*; example — *for instance, such as*; conclusion — *thus, in conclusion*.

**Choosing a title:** it must cover the **whole** passage — reject one that is **too broad** (the whole subject area) or **too narrow** (one detail).

**Don't confuse:** **sarcastic** (bitter mockery of a person/idea) with **satirical** (mocking society's folly to reform it); **didactic** (teaches a lesson) with **objective** (no lesson, no feeling).
keyPoints: Optimistic = hopeful; pessimistic = expecting the worst; nostalgic = longing for the past.
Sarcastic / ironic = saying the opposite to mock; satirical = mocking folly to correct it.
Didactic = teaching a moral lesson; objective = facts without feeling; laudatory = praising; sceptical = doubtful.
Author's purpose: inform, persuade, entertain, describe/explain.
Passage types: narrative (story), descriptive (scene), expository (explains), argumentative (argues).
Signal words: because/therefore (cause), however/whereas (contrast), for instance (example), thus (conclusion).
A good title covers the whole passage — neither too broad nor too narrow.
